title: Safiyyah and Maymunah
hook: Safiyyah, taunted for her Jewish family, is defended by the Prophet ﷺ, and Maymunah's house becomes a place where a boy learns the night prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Habibah, the folded bedding and the three days of mourning. Your line was: faith before family pride. Did you find a kind word for someone who sees it differently? Day eight hundred sixteen.

A woman is crying, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks in and asks why. Safiyyah tells him what she heard. Someone in the household, Hafsah, had called her the daughter of a Jew. It was meant to sting, and it did. Safiyyah came from a noble family of a Jewish tribe of Arabia, and that remark turned her family into an insult. What he says next is preserved in Tirmidhi's collection. Today: Safiyyah and Maymunah.
screen: `A WOMAN IN TEARS.` → `THE DAUGHTER OF A JEW?` → `WHAT HE SAYS NEXT.`

segments.voice: He doesn't tell Safiyyah to forget her family, or to be ashamed of it. He turns the taunt inside out. You are the daughter of a prophet, he tells her, meaning Aaron. Your uncle is a prophet, meaning Moses. And you are married to a prophet. So what is there for her to boast over you? Then he says: Hafsah, be mindful of Allah. Look at what he did. The very thing used against Safiyyah, her descent, became the thing he honored. The Qur'an names Aaron and Moses among the prophets, and Muslims honor them as such. He pointed her to that line and said: this is yours. A taunt about where she came from was answered by honoring where she came from. He defended her. Now Maymunah, the other name in today's title. Tradition remembers her as the last woman he married. One scene with her in it is gentle and ordinary. Her nephew, Abdullah ibn Abbas, still a boy, slept over at her house one night, and he tells us in Bukhari what he saw: the Prophet rising in the night, making his ablution, and standing to pray. The boy got up and stood beside him to join in. And the Prophet took hold of him and moved him around to his right side, where he should stand. Ibn Abbas grew up to be a teacher himself, and this lesson he learned in Maymunah's house. One wife, defended against a taunt. One wife whose home was open for a boy to learn. He defended her.
screen: `DAUGHTER OF A PROPHET, AARON.` · `YOUR UNCLE IS MOSES.` · `THE TAUNT TURNED INTO HONOR.` · `A BOY LEARNS IN MAYMUNAH'S HOUSE.` · then, large: `HE DEFENDED HER.`

segments.voice: The practice: defend someone from a taunt. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a remark you've heard aimed at someone's family, their background, their accent, their faith. Maybe in a group chat, maybe at work. Now find what the Prophet found: something true and good in the very thing they were mocked for. Hold that sentence until it's ready to say. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say it. The bell holds the time.
Safiyyah, taunted as the daughter of a Jew, and told by the Prophet that she was the daughter, niece, and wife of prophets. Today's word.
Your line: he defended her. Today, when someone is mocked for where they come from, say one true, good thing about it. Day eight hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Safiyyah bint Huyayy and Maymunah bint al-Harith among the mothers of the believers; the Prophet's answer to the taunt is retold from Jami' al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Abbas's night in Maymunah's house from Sahih al-Bukhari.

original.note: Arabic: the two names of today's mothers of the believers.

what it means: one defended against a taunt about her family, one whose home taught a boy to pray.
what a scholar hears: Tirmidhi 3894 for 'you are the daughter of a prophet'; Bukhari 138 for Ibn Abbas's night in Maymunah's house.
recall: listed the good he had done

sources.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3894 (Safiyyah taunted; 'you are the daughter of a prophet')
Sahih al-Bukhari 138 (Ibn Abbas spends the night at Maymunah's house; the night prayer; moved to the right side)
Qur'an 19:51–53 (Moses and Aaron named as prophets)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Tirmidhi 3894 and its grading.
'The biographers name her as the last woman he married' (Maymunah) is attributed, not asserted; confirm.
The Khaybar context of Safiyyah's marriage is deliberately left out; Keeper may wish to add careful context.
Ibn Abbas's age is not given; 'still a boy' only. The ear detail and right side: confirm against Bukhari's wording.
Check that the framing of the taunt honors Jewish descent and never uses Jews as a foil.

Editor: 'the last woman he married' is now 'tradition remembers', since no cited text says it; the ear detail is cut because Bukhari 138 only has him moved to the right; the taunt line now honors Safiyyah's descent without ranking it; 'turns to Hafsah' changed because Tirmidhi does not place her in the room.
